etymology.historical_story: Zeus is a Greek divine name, retained as a proper name when discussing ancient mythology. Greek art commonly identifies him through a thunderbolt, his characteristic weapon and symbol. Museum objects preserve this association across centuries, providing a useful cultural anchor for remembering the name without inventing a Malay root or an unsupported borrowing history. [Zeus in Greek art](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/251078)

senses.zh_definition: 民间传说或恐怖作品中复活并活动的死尸；现代虚构作品中也指具有类似特征的受感染者。

senses.ms_definition: Orang yang kelihatan lesu, kurang peka atau bertindak secara mekanis, misalnya akibat terlalu letih atau kurang tidur.

etymology.historical_story: The word family behind zombi is associated with Caribbean Creole forms such as zonbi and ultimately with Bantu vocabulary for spirits. International horror storytelling developed the familiar walking-dead image. Malay uses the spelling zombi, which DBP explicitly recommends as the equivalent of English zombie; this does not establish the precise historical route into Malay. [Merriam-Webster: zombie](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/zombie) [DBP: zombi](https://prpm.dbp.gov.my/Cari1?d=175768&keyword=horror)

etymology.historical_story: Zen is the Japanese reading of a Chinese Buddhist term, Chan, shortened from a transcription of Sanskrit dhyāna, meaning meditation. etymology.historical_story: Zarah comes from Arabic dharra, meaning a tiny particle or speck. Malay preserves that smallness in the everyday dust sense and uses the same word for scientific particles. Its Jawi spelling, ذره, also illustrates how an Arabic borrowing can acquire a conventional Malay written form. This connects a familiar image of dust with the less visible world described in physics. [Zarah: etymology](https://ms.wiktionary.org/wiki/zarah)

etymology.historical_story: Zat comes from Arabic dhāt, associated with essence or being. An early Malay vocabulary records both substance and divine essence, showing that its abstract meaning was already established. Modern Malay also uses it for constituents and nutrients, so the same short word can appear in discussions of theology, plant pigments and everyday meals. See [Shellabear's vocabulary](https://ms.wikisource.org/wiki/Malay-English_Vocabulary/Z).

etymology.historical_story: Zaitun reflects Arabic zaytūn, meaning olive trees and their fruit. The olive also has a notable place in Islamic scripture, which helps explain its cultural familiarity in Malay Muslim settings. In everyday Malay, the same base appears in buah zaitun and minyak zaitun, connecting the fruit with its familiar culinary oil. etymology.historical_story: Disney released Zootopia in 2016, using the same name for its film and its fictional animal metropolis. The spelling invites a connection between zoo and utopia; this is a transparent interpretation of the title, rather than a Malay derivation.
